props.title: The Wages of Fear
props.initialSlug: Four men risk death hauling volatile explosives

sections.content: The Wages of Fear (1953) revolutionized thriller filmmaking through pure existential tension. Director Henri-Georges Clouzot crafted a masterpiece about four desperate men driving trucks loaded with volatile nitroglycerin through treacherous South American mountain roads. The film's influence echoes through later high-stakes transport thrillers like Sorcerer (1977), William Friedkin's gritty remake, and Mad Max: Fury Road (2015). Clouzot's genius lies in stretching every moment of danger to breaking point - a bump in the road, a patch of oil, or a simple turn becomes unbearably tense when the slightest mistake means instant death.

sections.content: The film's brutal portrayal of corporate exploitation in Latin America hit hard in 1953 and remains relevant. American oil companies tried blocking its U.S. release, seeing themselves in the film's villainous Southern Oil Company. This anti-capitalist edge influenced later French thrillers like Z (1969) and inspired New Hollywood's cynical take on corporate power in films like Network (1976) and The China Syndrome (1979).

Clouzot's documentary-like attention to technical detail set a new standard for realism in action sequences. Each obstacle - crossing a rickety wooden platform, navigating hairpin turns, backing up on a narrow mountain road - is meticulously staged for maximum tension. This approach influenced everything from The French Connection (1971) to Duel (1971) and modern films like Sicario (2015). SUBHEAD: Legacy in Modern Cinema

movies.title: Rififi
movies.slug: A jewelry heist thriller famous for its 30-minute silent robbery sequence, showing Clouzot's influence on technical precision.

sections.content: The film's DNA runs through contemporary thrillers that trap characters in confined spaces with death literally inches away. Speed (1994) borrowed its "one wrong move means explosion" premise, while United 93 (2006) and Captain Phillips (2013) echo its documentary-style tension building. Even Christopher Nolan cited it as inspiration for the truck sequences in The Dark Knight (2008).
